question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

In the nick of time
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Only just in time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "in the nick of time" means at the very last moment before it is too late; only just in time. (ऐन मौके पर / ठीक समय पर)

◦ Example: The fireman reached the burning house in the nick of time and saved the child.

• The sense of the idiom is that of a narrow escape — something happens just before the deadline or disaster.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Frequently" means often/repeatedly — it expresses frequency, not timing.

• Option 3 "Every time" means on each occasion — again frequency, not a last-minute rescue.

• Option 4 "Meantime" means the period in between two events ("in the meantime") — unrelated to punctuality.

NOTE

• Related time idioms often asked in SSC: "against the clock" (in a hurry to finish before a deadline), "at the eleventh hour" (at the last possible moment), "high time" (the right time to act), "call it a day" (to stop work for the day).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

Pay attention to what's happening and make _______ adjustments based on your personal experience.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. reasonable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Reasonable" means sensible, fair and based on good judgement. "Make reasonable adjustments" is a natural and very common collocation — sensible changes made in the light of experience. (उचित / तर्कसंगत)

◦ Correct: Pay attention to what's happening and make reasonable adjustments based on your personal experience.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "impartial" means unbiased/neutral — it describes judges and decisions, not adjustments made from personal experience (indeed "personal experience" is the opposite of impartial evidence).

• Option 2 "honest" means truthful — one does not "make honest adjustments".

• Option 3 "placid" means calm and peaceful (used for lakes, temperaments) — it cannot describe adjustments.

NOTE

• Useful collocations with "adjustments": make/ making minor, slight, necessary, reasonable, seasonal adjustments. In SSC fill-in-the-blank questions, always test the option for collocation as well as meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

(Many a opportunities came and went while) he laid wasted.
option_1: Many an opportunity came and went while
option_3: Many an opportunities came and gone while
option_4: Many opportunities come and went as
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Many an opportunity came and went while.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The structure "Many a / Many an" is always followed by a singular countable noun and a singular verb, even though the meaning is plural.

◦ Structure: Many a/an + singular noun + singular verb.

◦ Correct: Many an opportunity came and went while he laid wasted.

• Since "opportunity" begins with a vowel sound, "many an" (not "many a") is used.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "No substitution required" is wrong because the printed segment "Many a opportunities" wrongly joins "many a" with a plural noun.

• Option 3 "Many an opportunities came and gone while" repeats the plural error and also uses "gone" (V3) where the past tense "went" is required after "came and".

• Option 4 "Many opportunities come and went as" mixes the present tense "come" with the past tense "went", which breaks tense parallelism.

NOTE

• Compare: "Many a student has passed" (singular verb) = "Many students have passed" (plural verb). Both are correct; the trap is mixing the two patterns.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

The participants responds to a series of statements at the dance competition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The participants responds.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This is an error of subject–verb agreement. The subject "The participants" is plural, so it must take the plural verb "respond", not the singular "responds".

◦ Correct: The participants respond to a series of statements at the dance competition.

• Rule: a singular subject takes a verb with "-s/-es" in the simple present (He responds); a plural subject takes the base verb (They respond).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "to a series of statements" is correct — "respond to" is the right preposition.

• Option 4 "at the dance competition" is correct — "at" is used for events and points/locations.

• Option 3 "No error" is wrong because a clear agreement error exists.

NOTE

• Watch the "a series of / a bunch of / a pack of" trap: the verb agrees with the head noun ("A series of lectures was organised"), not with the noun after "of".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

(Neither of the political factions have had much) interest in environmental intent.
option_2: Neither of the political factions have had any
option_3: Neither of the political faction has have much
option_4: Neither of the political factions has had much
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Neither of the political factions has had much.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Neither of + plural noun" is treated as singular, so it takes a singular verb: "Neither of the factions has", not "have".

◦ Correct: Neither of the political factions has had much interest in environmental intent.

• Similarly, "Either of / Each of / Neither of / None of (formal) / One of" + plural noun → singular verb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No substitution required" retains the plural verb "have had", which violates the rule.

• Option 2 also keeps "have had" and additionally changes "much" to "any" unnecessarily.

• Option 3 "has have much" is a double-verb construction and is grammatically impossible; it also wrongly uses the singular "faction" after "neither of the".

NOTE

• Remember the pair: "Neither ... nor" takes a verb agreeing with the nearer subject (Neither the boys nor the teacher is present), whereas "Neither of" is always singular.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Lumber has many _______ beyond home building.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. uses.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Uses" (plural of the noun "use") means the various purposes for which something can be employed. Lumber (sawn timber) has many uses apart from house construction — furniture, paper, packing crates, etc. (उपयोग)

◦ Correct: Lumber has many uses beyond home building.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "trunks" means the main stems of trees (or large boxes) — lumber is made from trunks; it does not "have trunks".

• Option 2 "loses" is a verb ("he loses"), not a noun, so it cannot follow "many"; the noun is "losses".

• Option 3 "pluses" means advantages/positive points — possible in casual speech but it does not fit "beyond home building", which clearly refers to additional applications.

NOTE

• Vocabulary: lumber/timber = wood prepared for building; log = an unsawn piece of trunk; plywood = layered wood board. Watch the spelling pair lose (verb, to misplace) and loose (adjective, not tight).

question:
The statement below has been given with bracketed text. Select the option with correct idiom for the bracketed text.

Don't start to think we've (won this game certainly), gentlemen.
option_4: got this game in the bag
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. got this game in the bag.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "(to have something) in the bag" means to be certain of winning or achieving something; as good as won. It exactly replaces "won this game certainly". (जीत निश्चित होना)

◦ Correct: Don't start to think we've got this game in the bag, gentlemen.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "swallowed the bitter truth" means accepted an unpleasant fact — the opposite mood of confident victory.

• Option 2 "held our horses" means waited patiently / slowed down — it does not convey certain victory.

• Option 3 "have skin in the game" means to have a personal stake or risk invested in something — not the same as being sure of winning.

NOTE

• Other "victory/confidence" idioms for SSC: "a walkover" (an easy win), "carry the day" (to win), "count your chickens before they hatch" (to assume success too early), "a done deal" (already settled).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym to substitute the bracketed word in the given sentence.

He is (frank) about what he sees as the shortcomings of his great predecessors.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. evasive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Frank" means open, honest and direct in speech; saying plainly what one thinks. (स्पष्टवादी)

• Its antonym is "evasive", which means avoiding a direct answer; not straightforward. (टालमटोल करने वाला)

◦ Example: The minister gave an evasive reply instead of a frank admission.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "assisting" means helping — unrelated to plain speaking.

• Option 2 "cheerful" means happy — an antonym of "gloomy", not of "frank".

• Option 4 "fortunate" means lucky — an antonym of "unlucky".

NOTE

• Synonyms of frank: candid, forthright, blunt, outspoken, straightforward. Antonyms: evasive, secretive, guarded, insincere, devious.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Many people may not find the rewards _______ with the time and effort required.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. commensurate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Commensurate" means in proportion to; matching in size, quality or degree. The fixed collocation is "commensurate with". (अनुरूप / समानुपाती)

◦ Correct: Many people may not find the rewards commensurate with the time and effort required — i.e., the rewards may not match the effort put in.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "collude" is a verb meaning to conspire secretly ("collude with") — a verb cannot follow "find the rewards" here.

• Option 2 "coffer" is a noun meaning a strongbox or a store of money ("the state coffers").

• Option 4 "capable" (able to do something) takes "of", not "with", and cannot describe rewards.

NOTE

• Preposition pairs worth remembering: commensurate with, compatible with, comparable to/with, proportionate to, consistent with. Salary advertisements often say "salary commensurate with experience".

question: Select the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Contribute.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Contribute" is the correct spelling. It means to give (money, help, ideas) towards a common purpose or result. (योगदान देना)

◦ Spelling key: CON + TRI + BUTE — one "r", one "b", and the ending "-bute".

◦ Example: Everyone was asked to contribute something to the relief fund.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "Contrribute" wrongly doubles the r; "Contribbute" wrongly doubles the b; "Contribuet" wrongly reverses the last two letters of "-bute".

NOTE

• Word family: contribute (verb), contribution (noun), contributor (person), contributory (adjective, as in "contributory negligence"). Related "-tribute" words: tribute, attribute, distribute, retribution.

question: Four sentences are given, out of which three have spelling errors. Choose the sentence with all correctly spelt words.
option_1: Microsoft announced plans to make bids to accquire Byte Dance.
option_2: The job of the artist is to make the revolution perceptible.
option_3: Except that it'll be rooted in awkard, funny and compelling reality.
option_4: She used the 14th Amendment to acheive equality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The job of the artist is to make the revolution perceptible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 2 is correctly spelt. "Perceptible" means able to be seen or noticed. (बोधगम्य / दृष्टिगोचर)

◦ Spelling key: PER + CEP + TIBLE (it ends in "-ible", not "-able").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "accquire" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "acquire" (a-c-q-u-i-r-e), with a single "c".

• Option 3: "awkard" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "awkward" (with a "w" before the "a-r-d").

• Option 4: "acheive" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "achieve", which follows the rule "i before e except after c".

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: acquire, achieve, awkward, occurrence, embarrass, maintenance, questionnaire, privilege, separate, definitely, receive.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Golden
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Shining.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Golden" means made of gold, or having the bright, gleaming, lustrous colour of gold. Its closest synonym among the options is "Shining" (bright and glowing). (सुनहरा / चमकीला)

◦ Example: The golden/shining dome of the temple glittered in the sunlight.

• Figuratively, "golden" also means excellent or precious — a "golden opportunity", the "golden age".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Dull" (not bright, lacking shine) is an antonym.

• Option 2 "Gloomy" (dark and depressing) is also opposite in sense.

• Option 4 "Dark" (without light) is a clear antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of golden/shining: gleaming, glittering, radiant, lustrous, brilliant, resplendent. Antonyms: dull, dim, tarnished, murky.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

The NCGG has been/ set up to assist in / bring about governance reforms through studies.
option_2: bring about governance reforms through studies.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. bring about governance reforms through studies.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition "in" at the end of the previous segment must be followed by a gerund (V-ing), not the base form of the verb. So "assist in bring about" is wrong; it must be "assist in bringing about".

◦ Correct: The NCGG has been set up to assist in bringing about governance reforms through studies.

• Rule: Preposition + V-ing (gerund) — "good at swimming", "interested in reading", "insist on going", "assist in preparing".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "The NCGG has been" is correct (present perfect passive with "set up").

• Option 1 "set up to assist in" is correct in itself — the error appears only when the next word fails to take the "-ing" form.

• Option 4 "No error" is wrong because a definite error exists.

NOTE

• Beware of the trap word "to": in "look forward to, object to, be used to, with a view to", the "to" is a preposition, so it too takes V-ing ("I look forward to meeting you").

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

I try to eat less meat and more vegetables.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined part "to eat less" is already correct.

◦ After "try", the to-infinitive is used, and an infinitive always takes the base form (V1) — "to eat".

◦ "Less" is the correct quantifier for uncountable nouns such as "meat" (less water, less sugar, less meat), whereas "fewer" is used with countable nouns (fewer books).

• Correct: I try to eat less meat and more vegetables.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "to eats less" is wrong — no "-s" is added to a verb after "to".

• Option 2 "to eat lesser" is wrong — "lesser" means "smaller in importance/value" (the lesser evil) and is not used for quantity of food.

• Option 3 "to ate less" is wrong — the past tense "ate" cannot follow "to".

NOTE

• Quantity pairs: much/less/little with uncountables; many/fewer/few with countables; more works with both. "Amount of" (uncountable) vs "number of" (countable).

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Eddie just panics/ when it gets close/ nearer the end.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. nearer the end.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "nearer the end" is faulty. The sentence already contains "close" in the previous segment, so putting the comparative "nearer" beside it creates a double/redundant comparison and leaves "close" without its required preposition "to".

◦ Correct: Eddie just panics when it gets close to the end. (or: ... when it gets nearer to the end.)

• Rule: the adjective "close" is followed by "to" — close to the door, close to the truth, close to the end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 4 "Eddie just panics" is correct — singular subject with singular verb "panics".

• Option 3 "when it gets close" is correct in itself; the fault lies in the segment that follows it.

• Option 2 "No error" is wrong because the third segment is clearly defective.

NOTE

• Spelling point: verbs ending in "-ic" add "k" before "-ed/-ing": panic → panicked, panicking; picnic → picnicked; traffic → trafficking.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

The only one _______ shattered their monotony by his visits was Krishna.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. who ever.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a relative pronoun acting as the subject of the verb "shattered", and it refers to a person ("The only one ... was Krishna"). The subject form for a person is "who"; "ever" is added for emphasis.

◦ Correct: The only one who ever shattered their monotony by his visits was Krishna.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "whom ever" is wrong — "whom" is the object form; here the pronoun performs the action (it is followed directly by the verb "shattered").

• Options 2 "whatever" and 4 "which ever" are used for things, not for a person.

NOTE

• Quick test: if the pronoun is followed by a verb, use "who"; if it is followed by a subject + verb, use "whom". Compare: "the man who called me" / "the man whom I called".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Irreverent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Respectful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Irreverent" means showing a lack of respect for people or things that are generally taken seriously. (अनादरपूर्ण / अश्रद्धालु)

• Its antonym is "Respectful", meaning showing deference and regard. (आदरपूर्ण)

◦ Example: His irreverent jokes about the ceremony upset the elders, who expected a respectful silence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Restoration" is a noun meaning the act of restoring something to its former state — not an antonym.

• Option 3 "Dormant" means inactive or sleeping (a dormant volcano).

• Option 4 "Relevant" means closely connected with the matter in hand — it is the antonym of "irrelevant", a look-alike trap word.

NOTE

• Note the prefix "ir-" (a form of "in-" used before "r") meaning "not": irreverent, irrelevant, irregular, irresponsible, irrational, irresistible.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

One who hates or discriminates against women.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Misogynist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Misogynist" is a person who hates, dislikes or is strongly prejudiced against women. (स्त्री-द्वेषी)

◦ Word roots: Greek miso- = hatred + gyne = woman.

◦ Example: The novel exposes the misogynist attitudes of its era.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Pessimist" — one who always expects the worst.

• Option 3 "Feminist" — one who supports equal rights for women (the near-opposite of a misogynist).

• Option 4 "Atheist" — one who does not believe in the existence of God.

NOTE

• Related "miso-" words: misandrist (one who hates men), misanthrope (one who hates mankind), misogamist (one who hates marriage). Other useful one-word substitutes: misogyny (the hatred itself), philanthropist (a lover of mankind).

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

A violent wind that has a circular movement
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Hurricane.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Hurricane" is a violent storm with a strong, circular (rotating) wind system, formed over warm tropical oceans. (चक्रवाती तूफ़ान)

◦ Example: The hurricane uprooted trees and flattened houses along the coast.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Drought" — a long period of abnormally low rainfall / water scarcity.

• Option 2 "Deluge" — a great flood or a very heavy downpour of rain.

• Option 3 "Tsunami" — a series of enormous sea waves caused by an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption, not by wind.

NOTE

• Static-GK link: the same rotating tropical storm is called a hurricane in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, a typhoon in the north-western Pacific, and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean region. A small violent land whirlwind is a tornado.

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

I am parched, dehydrated to the point of pain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Drained.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dehydrated" means having lost water or moisture; dried out. Its closest synonym here is "Drained", meaning emptied of liquid / having the moisture removed. (निर्जलित / सूखा हुआ)

◦ The context word "parched" (extremely dry, very thirsty) confirms this sense of severe loss of water.

◦ Example: After hours in the sun the trekkers were completely dehydrated/drained.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Braced" means prepared or steadied oneself for something difficult.

• Option 2 "Moistened" (made slightly wet) is a clear antonym of dehydrated.

• Option 4 "Washed" means cleaned with water — it involves adding water, not losing it.

NOTE

• Synonyms of dehydrated: parched, desiccated, arid, drained, dried up. Antonyms: hydrated, moistened, saturated, drenched. Prefix "de-" = removal (dehydrate, defrost, deforest, devalue).

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

The figure of Arthur first appeared in Welsh poetry in the (1) ______ sixth and early seventh centuries, a hero who was (2) ______ lead the Britons in battle against Saxon invaders. But it wasn't (3) _______ the 12th century that he was first tied to this dramatic headland, known as Tintagel. The timeless popularity of the Arthur legend has overshadowed a central, unresolved (4) _______: Was there really a King Arthur, or at least a historical prototype upon whom Geoffrey's hero is (5) ______?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. late.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is balanced against the words "and early seventh centuries" later in the same phrase. The natural pairing is "the late sixth and early seventh centuries" — i.e., the closing part of the 6th century and the opening part of the 7th.

◦ Correct: The figure of Arthur first appeared in Welsh poetry in the late sixth and early seventh centuries ...

• "Late" before a period of time means "towards the end of" (the late 1990s, the late Middle Ages) and is the direct opposite of "early".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "least" is the superlative of "little" and makes no sense with a century.

• Option 3 "latest" means "most recent" — it cannot describe a century in the distant past.

• Option 4 "latter" means "the second of two things already mentioned" and needs a prior pair to refer back to.

NOTE

• Contrast pairs used with periods: early / late, the turn of the century, mid- (the mid-nineteenth century). Note "later" (afterwards) versus "latter" (the second of two).

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

The figure of Arthur first appeared in Welsh poetry in the (1) ______ sixth and early seventh centuries, a hero who was (2) ______ lead the Britons in battle against Saxon invaders. But it wasn't (3) _______ the 12th century that he was first tied to this dramatic headland, known as Tintagel. The timeless popularity of the Arthur legend has overshadowed a central, unresolved (4) _______: Was there really a King Arthur, or at least a historical prototype upon whom Geoffrey's hero is (5) ______?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. said to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passive structure "be said to + V1" means it is reported/believed that somebody does something. Since Arthur is a legendary figure whose deeds are only reported, this is exactly the sense required.

◦ Correct: ... a hero who was said to lead the Britons in battle against Saxon invaders.

◦ Structure: Subject + is/was said to + base verb — "He is said to be very rich."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "tamed to" (made docile) is meaningless with "lead the Britons".

• Option 3 "brought to" would need an object ("brought to justice") and does not fit before a base verb.

• Option 4 "told" is wrong because "was told lead" is ungrammatical — it would need "was told to lead", which also changes the meaning to receiving an order.

NOTE

• Similar reporting structures: "is believed to", "is supposed to", "is known to", "is thought to", "is reputed to". They are common in news and historical writing.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

The figure of Arthur first appeared in Welsh poetry in the (1) ______ sixth and early seventh centuries, a hero who was (2) ______ lead the Britons in battle against Saxon invaders. But it wasn't (3) _______ the 12th century that he was first tied to this dramatic headland, known as Tintagel. The timeless popularity of the Arthur legend has overshadowed a central, unresolved (4) _______: Was there really a King Arthur, or at least a historical prototype upon whom Geoffrey's hero is (5) ______?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. until.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed emphatic pattern is "It wasn't until + time + that + clause", meaning not before that time did the event happen.

◦ Correct: But it wasn't until the 12th century that he was first tied to this dramatic headland, known as Tintagel.

◦ Sense: only in the 12th century was Arthur first linked to Tintagel — not earlier.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "none" is a pronoun and cannot be followed by "the 12th century that ...".

• Option 2 "beyond" means "on the far side of / later than" and destroys the intended "not before" meaning.

• Option 4 "unless" means "if not" and introduces a condition, not a point of time.

NOTE

• Related cleft structures for emphasis: "It was only in 1947 that India became independent", "Not until the results came out did he relax" (note the inversion after a negative opening).

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

The figure of Arthur first appeared in Welsh poetry in the (1) ______ sixth and early seventh centuries, a hero who was (2) ______ lead the Britons in battle against Saxon invaders. But it wasn't (3) _______ the 12th century that he was first tied to this dramatic headland, known as Tintagel. The timeless popularity of the Arthur legend has overshadowed a central, unresolved (4) _______: Was there really a King Arthur, or at least a historical prototype upon whom Geoffrey's hero is (5) ______?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. question.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The colon after the blank is followed by an actual interrogative sentence — "Was there really a King Arthur ...?" So the noun before the colon must be "question".

◦ Correct: ... has overshadowed a central, unresolved question: Was there really a King Arthur ...?

• The adjective "unresolved" also collocates naturally with "question", "issue" and "dispute".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "establishment" means an organisation or the act of setting something up.

• Option 2 "commotion" means noisy confusion or disturbance.

• Option 3 "mess" means an untidy or difficult state of affairs — too informal and not something that a colon-introduced question can explain.

NOTE

• Punctuation point: a colon (:) introduces an explanation, a list or, as here, the exact content of what has just been named. Collocations: an open/vexed/burning/unresolved question.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

The figure of Arthur first appeared in Welsh poetry in the (1) ______ sixth and early seventh centuries, a hero who was (2) ______ lead the Britons in battle against Saxon invaders. But it wasn't (3) _______ the 12th century that he was first tied to this dramatic headland, known as Tintagel. The timeless popularity of the Arthur legend has overshadowed a central, unresolved (4) _______: Was there really a King Arthur, or at least a historical prototype upon whom Geoffrey's hero is (5) ______?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. based.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence asks whether there was a real person "upon whom Geoffrey's hero is ...". The idiomatic phrase is "to be based upon/on somebody or something", meaning to be modelled on / derived from.

◦ Correct: ... or at least a historical prototype upon whom Geoffrey's hero is based?

◦ Example: The film is based on a true story.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "caged" (shut in a cage) makes no sense with "upon whom".

• Option 3 "hanged" refers to execution by hanging and does not take "upon whom".

• Option 4 "found" would require "in whom"/"by whom" and would not convey the idea of a model or prototype.

NOTE

• Note the verb pair: "hanged" is used only for execution (the convict was hanged), while "hung" is used for objects (the picture was hung). Collocation: "based on/upon", "modelled on", "drawn from".
